lessons.title: Welding safety
lessons.html:
Joining metal on the farm

Welding joins two pieces of metal by melting them together. In farm equipment repair you may weld a cracked implement frame, a broken bracket, a trailer drawbar repair or a gate. Other joining methods include brazing, soldering, bolting and riveting. This unit focuses on basic arc welding (stick or MIG) under supervision.

Hazards

  • Arc light: ultraviolet and infrared light can burn your eyes (arc eye or welder's flash) and skin, even in a few seconds.
  • Electric shock: from damaged cables, wet conditions or touching live parts.
  • Burns: from hot metal, sparks and spatter.
  • Fumes: welding fumes can harm the lungs. Galvanised or painted metal gives off especially harmful fumes.
  • Fire: sparks can travel far and set fire to grass, oil, rags, fuel or dry chaff.

Protective equipment

  • Welding helmet with the correct shade filter lens
  • Leather welding gloves
  • Flame-resistant overalls or leather jacket, with no frayed edges or open pockets
  • Safety boots and leather spats
  • Safety glasses under the helmet for chipping and grinding
  • Respiratory protection where fumes cannot be removed by ventilation

Safe workplace

  • Clear flammable material away from the welding area. Never weld near fuel tanks, diesel bowsers or containers that held fuel or chemicals.
  • Use welding screens to protect other people from the arc.
  • Ensure good ventilation or fume extraction.
  • Keep a fire extinguisher close and watch for fires for some time after finishing.
  • Keep the work area and yourself dry.

Welding on machines

Before welding on a tractor or implement, disconnect the battery or follow the manufacturer's instructions to protect electronics. Place the earth clamp close to the weld so current does not pass through bearings or electronic parts. Never weld on a wheel rim with a tyre fitted, and never weld on hydraulic cylinders or pressurised parts.

lessons.title: Equipment and preparation
lessons.html:
Getting ready to weld

Welding machines

ProcessHow it worksFarm use
Stick (MMA / SMAW)A coated electrode melts to form the weld; the coating makes a gas shield and slagOutdoor repairs, thicker steel, rusty or dirty metal
MIG / MAG (GMAW)A wire feeds through the gun with shielding gas from a cylinderWorkshop work, thinner sheet, faster welding

Checking equipment

  • Inspect cables for cuts or damaged insulation.
  • Check that the electrode holder or MIG gun is in good condition.
  • Check that the earth clamp is clean and grips firmly.
  • For MIG, check the gas cylinder is chained upright and the regulator works.
  • Report and do not use damaged equipment.

Selecting electrodes and settings

The electrode type and size depend on the metal and thickness. Thicker metal needs a bigger electrode and more current. Follow the electrode maker's recommended current range on the packet, and the welding machine chart. Store electrodes dry; damp electrodes give poor welds.

Preparing the metal

  1. Identify the metal. Most farm implements are mild steel. Cast iron, stainless steel and aluminium need special methods; ask your mentor.
  2. Clean the joint area to bright metal: remove paint, rust, oil and galvanising with a grinder or wire brush.
  3. Prepare the edges. Thicker plate may need a bevel so the weld penetrates fully.
  4. Fit up the pieces with the correct gap and alignment. Use clamps, magnets or a jig.
  5. Tack weld at a few points to hold the pieces in place, then check alignment before the full weld.

Joint types

  • Butt joint: two pieces edge to edge.
  • Lap joint: one piece overlapping another.
  • T-joint (fillet): one piece at right angles to another.
  • Corner joint: two pieces meeting at a corner.

lessons.title: Making and checking the weld
lessons.html:
Welding technique

Striking and running the arc (stick)

  1. Put on all PPE and lower your helmet before striking.
  2. Strike the arc by scratching or tapping the electrode on the metal.
  3. Hold a short arc length, about the same as the electrode core diameter.
  4. Tilt the electrode slightly in the direction of travel.
  5. Move at a steady speed so the weld pool stays the same size.
  6. At the end, fill the crater before breaking the arc.
  7. Chip off the slag with a chipping hammer while wearing safety glasses, then wire brush.

MIG technique

  • Keep the correct stick-out of wire from the nozzle.
  • Hold the gun at a steady angle and distance.
  • Shield the area from wind, which blows away the gas.

Checking the weld

A good weld is even in width and height, has smooth ripples, blends into the metal on both sides and has no holes or cracks.

DefectWhat it looks likeCommon cause
PorositySmall holes in the weldDirty metal, damp electrodes, poor gas shield
UndercutGroove along the edge of the weldCurrent too high, wrong angle
Lack of fusionWeld sits on top without joiningCurrent too low, moving too fast
Slag inclusionSlag trapped in the weldNot cleaning between runs
Excess spatterMany small balls around the weldCurrent too high, long arc

Welds on safety-critical parts, such as drawbars, hitches, lifting points and axles, must be inspected by a qualified person. Some parts should be replaced, not welded. Ask your mentor.

After welding

  • Let hot parts cool, or mark them HOT.
  • Switch off the machine and close gas cylinders.
  • Roll up cables and store equipment.
  • Check the area for smouldering fires.
  • Prime and paint the weld area to stop rust.

Key points

  • Arc light burns eyes and skin; always use the correct helmet and PPE.
  • Clear flammables away and keep a fire extinguisher near.
  • Disconnect the battery and place the earth clamp close to the weld on machines.
  • Clean metal to bright steel and tack before full welding.
  • Hold a short arc and steady speed; check for porosity, undercut and lack of fusion.
  • Safety-critical welds must be inspected by a qualified person.
